newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Biggest N.Korean defector group arrives in Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Biggest N.Korean defector group arrives in Seoul.

text.p: The biggest group of North Korean defectors since the 1950-53 Korean War arrived in Seoul on Monday to take up asylum, six weeks after making a dramatic escape through China and Hong Kong.
The 17 refugees were all related and included a security guard whose job was to stop such defectors fleeing through the isolated North Korea-China border.

Their escape was financed by relatives in the United States who sent money to pay for guides to protect the group during the month-long trek down the length of China. They were passed from one safe house to another among the two million ethnic Koreans living there.

In a sign of changing times and growing nervousness about what a North Korean collapse could mean for Seoul's economy, the reception was low-key. Only a small crowd of mainly relatives was at Seoul's airport for the group's arrival on a Korean Airlines flight from Hong Kong.

South Korea will offer the family asylum and a modest payment. Seoul media have speculated each person will receive about 10 million won ($12,000) to help them settle and find work, a sum that will not go far in high-cost South Korea.
On the eve of the group's departure from Hong Kong, South Korean media reports said two other North Koreans were also in the British colony waiting their turn for asylum in Seoul.

The sudden spate of refugees has put an unwelcome spotlight on Hong Kong as an escape centre for North Koreans just as the British colony enters the final months of its handover to China, one of Pyongyang's few allies.
"These cases are not the sort of problem they (British authorities in Hong Kong) need when they're tidying up the house," one Western diplomat said. "Its an awkward problem."
Most of the 17 escapees, who sneaked into Hong Kong 16 days ago after making their escape from North Korea on October 26, looked sombre.
Earlier reports had said the security guard was not a member of the family, but during questioning it emerged he was related and was the ringleader of the group in their flight.
South Korea once rolled out the red carpet for defectors, but their growing number is starting to cause concern that a sudden crackup of the Stalinist nation is possible.
Some recent defectors have been weak and emaciated, reflecting near-famine conditions in much of the North, which is struggling to survive the effects of floods and industrial collapse.

An uncontrolled refugee exodus, signalling a breakdown of internal controls -- similar to the German experience -- is part of a nightmare scenario for Seoul, which would be left to pick up the pieces from any collapse in the North.

The South Korean government is drawing up plans for reception centres for North Koreans, half-way houses that will offer immediate shelter and vocational training. The first such centre could be ready next year.
